title: Modulation
intro: A modulation moves the tonal centre to a new key, confirmed by a cadence there. Most modulations go to closely related keys, and most use a pivot chord that belongs to both keys.

blocks.text: The closely related keys of a major key are its relative minor and the keys a fifth above and below with their relatives: from C major, A minor, G major, E minor, F major and D minor. Their key signatures differ by at most one sharp or flat, and their tonic triads are all diatonic chords of the home key (vi, V, iii, IV, ii). In a minor key the most common destination is the relative major (A minor → C major); in a major key, the dominant (C → G).

A pivot chord is a chord diatonic in both keys, which the ear reinterprets. To go from C to G: Am is vi in C and ii in G. The progression C–Am–D7–G treats Am as vi on arrival and as ii looking back, then D7 (V7 in G, with F♯) confirms the new key, and a cadence in G completes the modulation. In analysis the pivot gets two labels: vi = ii.

widget.title: C major to G major via the pivot Am (vi = ii)

items: Direct (phrase) modulation: the new key simply starts with the next phrase, no pivot. Common in hymns and pop.
Chromatic pivot: a chord that is chromatic in one key, often a secondary dominant or borrowed chord, becomes diatonic in the other.

Common-tone modulation: a single held note links two distantly related keys (A♭ held, reinterpreted from 3̂ of F minor to 1̂ of A♭ major, or to 3̂ of E major as G♯). Schubert and Brahms used this for sudden changes of light.

Enharmonic modulation: a diminished seventh or German augmented sixth chord respelled, so it resolves in an unexpected key. Each note of a diminished seventh can act as a leading tone, so one diminished seventh can lead to four different keys.
The 'truck driver's' key change: in pop, the last chorus moved up a semitone or whole tone with no preparation, for a lift in energy.

blocks.text: Practise modulating to each closely related key from C with a four-chord pattern: tonic, pivot, new V7, new tonic. Then try common-tone modulations by holding one note in the right hand and changing the harmony under it.

blocks.title: Pivots
blocks.text: Find a pivot chord between D major and A major, and between D major and B minor.
solution: D major chords: D, Em, F♯m, G, A, Bm, C♯°. A major chords: A, Bm, C♯m, D, E, F♯m, G♯°. Shared: D (I = IV), F♯m (iii = vi), A (V = I), Bm (vi = ii). The best pivot is a predominant in the new key: Bm (vi in D = ii in A).
B minor chords (harmonic): Bm, C♯°, D, Em, F♯, G, A♯°. Shared with D major: D (I = III), Em (ii = iv), G (IV = VI), Bm (vi = i). A good pivot: Em (ii = iv) or G (IV = VI).
blocks.answer: Bm (vi = ii); Em (ii = iv) or G (IV = VI)

blocks.title: Closely related
blocks.text: List the closely related keys of E minor.
solution: E minor has one sharp. Keys with zero, one or two sharps and tonic triads diatonic to E minor: G major (relative), A minor (iv), C major (VI), B minor (v), D major (VII).

McGraw-Hill; Laitz, S. G. (2016). The Complete Musician, 4th ed. Oxford University Press; Temperley, D. (2018). The Musical Language of Rock. Oxford University Press.
